claims.claim: Microsoft links hyperscale compute infrastructure and frontier-model capacity to enterprise software, developer tools and cloud services; Azure scale and 30M+ paid Microsoft 365 Copilot seats show demand on both infrastructure and application layers.

The causal bottleneck is not AI demand alone but converting capital-intensive compute capacity into durable utilization and software economics; commercial RPO provides demand visibility but does not by itself prove returns on the current infrastructure wave.

risks.risk: Successor bottlenecks include power, datacenter capacity and return conversion on AI infrastructure; high demand can coexist with weaker economics if capital intensity outruns monetization.

unknowns.unknown: Current evidence does not isolate returns on AI infrastructure from broader Azure economics.

claims.claim: The strongest present challenge is economic rather than demand-side: AI infrastructure intensity is pressuring cloud gross margin and free-cash-flow conversion while Microsoft commits substantial capital ahead of fully observable returns.

Commercial RPO and Copilot adoption strengthen the demand thesis but should not be treated as proof that AI capex will earn superior incremental returns; the thesis is falsified if utilization/monetization fails to offset sustained capital intensity and margin pressure.

risks.risk: Capital intensity and infrastructure concentration can reduce returns if AI demand converts more slowly or competitively priced substitutes compress economics.

unknowns.unknown: Incremental AI workload margins and stand-alone returns on the current infrastructure build are not disclosed in the reused evidence.
